title: Binary Searchable Numbers in an Unsorted Array
statement:
Consider a search procedure that looks for a value `target` inside a sequence of integers:

1. While the sequence still has elements, pick any one of them as the pivot (the choice is arbitrary and may differ from run to run).
2. If the pivot equals `target`, the search succeeds.
3. If the pivot is smaller than `target`, delete the pivot together with every element before it.
4. If the pivot is larger than `target`, delete the pivot together with every element after it.
5. If the sequence runs out, the search fails.

On a sorted sequence this always finds a value that is present, but on an unsorted one some pivot choices can throw the value away. You are given `nums`, an array of distinct integers that may or may not be sorted. Return how many values of `nums` are certain to be found when the procedure searches `nums` for them, whatever pivots it picks.
constraints: All values in nums are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Follow the search for the value at index `i`. A pivot to its left is harmless only if it is smaller (then it and the elements before it go, and `nums[i]` survives). A pivot to its right is harmless only if it is larger. If any element on the left is larger, or any element on the right is smaller, the search can pick that one first and throw `nums[i]` away. So `nums[i]` is guaranteed exactly when it is bigger than everything before it and smaller than everything after it. Simulating every pivot order is exponential; two running extremes answer the question in linear time.

## Approach

1. Build `suffixMin`, where `suffixMin[i]` is the smallest value from index `i` to the end (`Infinity` past the end).
2. Walk left to right, keeping `prefixMax`, the largest value seen before `i`.
3. If `nums[i]` beats `prefixMax` and is below `suffixMin[i + 1]`, add one to `count`.
4. Fold `nums[i]` into `prefixMax` and continue; return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [7]`. The suffix pass gives `suffixMin = [7, Infinity]`. At `i = 0`, `prefixMax` is `-Infinity`, so `7 > -Infinity`, and `suffixMin[1]` is `Infinity`, so `7 < Infinity`: `count` becomes 1, and the answer is `1`. (In Example 2, `[-1, 5, 2]`, only `-1` passes: `5` has the smaller `2` after it and `2` has the larger `5` before it.)

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one backward pass and one forward pass.
- Space: O(n) for `suffixMin`.

## Pitfalls

- Compare with the minimum strictly **after** `i` (`suffixMin[i + 1]`), not one that includes `nums[i]` itself.
- Update `prefixMax` after the test, so it covers only the elements before `i`.
- Use `-Infinity` and `Infinity` (or values beyond the range) as sentinels so the first and last elements are judged correctly.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `suffixMin` | `suffixMin[i]` is the smallest value in `nums[i..n-1]` |
| `prefixMax` | largest value strictly before the current index |
| `count` | values found so far that are guaranteed to be found |
| `i` | current index |

narration.3: Prepare a suffix-minimum array with Infinity past the end, so the last element has nothing smaller after it.
narration.4: Walk from right to left to fill the suffix minimums.
narration.5: The smallest value from i onward is the smaller of nums[i] and the minimum after it.
narration.8: No element comes before index 0, so the running maximum starts at -Infinity.
narration.10: Now walk left to right, testing each value.
narration.11: A value is safe only if it beats everything before it and is below everything after it.
narration.12: Every pivot choice keeps this value, so count it.
narration.14: Include nums[i] in the maximum of the prefix before moving on.
narration.16: Return how many values are guaranteed to be found.
